articles.title: Nobody Uses Your AI Feature
articles.excerpt: Why adoption, not accuracy, decides whether an enterprise AI feature succeeds The launch went well. The demo impressed the management team. The evaluation scores were good. The feature was fast, secur…
articles.body: Why adoption, not accuracy, decides whether an enterprise AI feature succeeds The launch went well. The demo impressed the management team. The evaluation scores were good. The feature was fast, secure, and properly integrated with the CRM. The release notes went out on a Monday. Three months later, someone finally looked at the usage dashboard. A handful of people used it every day. Most had tried it once or twice. Many had never clicked the button at all. Nothing was broken. The feature simply didn't become part of anyone's work. This is a hypothetical example, but I suspect many teams building AI features in 2026 will recognize it. For the last few months, I have been writing mostly about architecture: state, security, cost, evaluation, model upgrades, master data, latency.

articles.title: Keeping MEF composition intact under obfuscation
articles.excerpt: A MEF plugin host has a failure mode that never raises an exception. You obfuscate the solution, ship it, and the host starts up reporting zero plugins — not because a type failed to load, but because…
articles.body: A MEF plugin host has a failure mode that never raises an exception. You obfuscate the solution, ship it, and the host starts up reporting zero plugins — not because a type failed to load, but because container.GetExports<IPlugin>() matched nothing and returned an empty sequence. MEF treats "no matching export" as an ordinary result, so there is no stack trace to follow. The composition contract moved, and the only symptom is absence. The reason is worth understanding exactly, because the fix is precise and the wrong fix — exclude the whole plugin assembly from renaming — throws away the protection you wanted. MEF does not compose by type. It composes by a contract-name string , and by default that string is derived from the contract type's full name.

articles.title: I Built a WCAG Color Contrast Checker That Runs Entirely in the Browser
articles.excerpt: Every developer has shipped text that looked fine on their monitor and was unreadable for someone else. WCAG contrast ratios exist to take the guesswork out of that — but most checkers online are eith…
articles.body: Every developer has shipped text that looked fine on their monitor and was unreadable for someone else. WCAG contrast ratios exist to take the guesswork out of that — but most checkers online are either buried in ads or ask you to install something. So I built one that runs 100% in the browser: pick a text color and a background color, and it instantly shows the contrast ratio, AA/AAA pass-fail badges for normal and large text, and a live preview. No server, no uploads, nothing leaves the page. Here is what I learned building it. The formula is simpler than it looks A contrast ratio is just a comparison of relative luminance — how bright a color actually appears, weighted the way human vision works (we are far more sensitive to green than to blue).

articles.title: Why Software Projects Get Delayed: 8 Alignment Gaps
articles.excerpt: When a software project slips, people usually look for a technical cause first: a hard integration, a stubborn bug, a slow developer. Sometimes that's the real reason. In my experience as a technical…
articles.body: When a software project slips, people usually look for a technical cause first: a hard integration, a stubborn bug, a slow developer. Sometimes that's the real reason. In my experience as a technical project manager, though, most delays start much earlier, with an alignment gap : two people who believed they agreed on something, and didn't. Current research points the same way. PMI's 2026 Pulse of the Profession lists misaligned objectives, unclear governance, and siloed teams among the forces that make projects complex. It also found that high performers are more likely to agree with sponsors on what success looks like before execution begins. My own biggest early mistakes came from exactly this: communication gaps and not aligning things properly.

articles.title: How moon dust and recycled cardboard could help NASA build its lunar base
articles.excerpt: The high cost of building on the moon has led to wide-ranging research on how to make use of the moon's most plentiful resource: the dusty regolith that covers its surface.
articles.body: The high cost of building on the moon has led to wide-ranging research on how to make use of the moon's most plentiful resource: the dusty regolith that covers its surface. Right now, lunar shipping runs about $544,000 per pound ($1.2 million per kilogram), so anything that astronauts can make on the moon using existing materials could help a lot. Scientists have already proposed using regolith for building 3D-printed bricks , solar arrays , and even as soil to grow potatoes . Now, a team of researchers from Purdue University in Indiana have developed an aerogel made from simulated regolith for insulating lunar habitats. New aerogels created by Purdue University researchers, made of cellulose and lunar regolith simulant, could pave the way for insulating materials made on the moon.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 28, 1967: Astronomers Jocelyn Bell and Antony Hewish disover the 1st pulsar with Little Green Men 1 signal
articles.excerpt: On November 28, 1967, astronomers found the first pulsar and they called the signal Little Green Men 1. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On November 28, 1967, astronomers found the first pulsar. A pulsar is a super-dense star that rotates super fast. As the pulsar spins, it emits two beams of light in opposite directions. When astronomers look at a pulsar, it looks like a star that's flickering on and off at a steady, constant pace. The first pulsar was observed by Jocelyn Bell Burnell and Antony Hewish. They were looking at the constellation Vulpecula when they saw a star flickering with regular pulses separated by 1.33 seconds. At first they had no idea what it was, so they jokingly nicknamed the signal Little Green Men 1. After more pulsars were discovered, they were able to rule out aliens. This chart tracked the signal of the first pulsar ever discoverered on Nov. 28, 1967.

articles.body: The 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade is sure to be a blast, but it is a bit light on "space." According to previews provided by the department store chain, the founder of the New York City holiday celebration, space fans turning up or tuning in to catch sight of an astronaut or other nod to NASA will have only a returning rocket to look forward to on Saturday (Nov. 28). (The parade has been postponed two days from Thursday, Nov. 26, due to bad weather.) Not that Macy's (or the space agency) has hinted about anything cosmic planned for the 100th parade; it's only that the event has had a long history of celebrating space exploration with its floats and balloons.
